commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Duke to YY; add greeting and exit message
AGENTS.md: fill in student experience and IDE placeholders
Add present-changes-visually skill for generating visual HTML diffs
Add support for marking tasks as done
Add support for unmarking tasks as done

commitResults.messageBody:
The project had no documented Java style convention, leaving
formatting and naming choices ad hoc as more code gets written.

Add the seedu-java-coding-standard skill, which codifies the SE-EDU
intermediate Java coding standard (naming, layout, statements, and
Javadoc conventions) as an actionable checklist. Reference it from
AGENTS.md so it is applied to all Java code in this project going
forward, not just remembered informally.

Commit messages so far have been written ad hoc, with no shared rule
for subject-line length, mood, or when a body is warranted.

Add the seedu-git-standard skill, which codifies the SE-EDU Git
conventions (subject/body formatting, imperative mood, one logical
change per commit) as an actionable checklist. Reference it from
AGENTS.md so it governs all commit messages written for this project
from now on.

YY currently tracks each task as a String, with a parallel boolean
array recording whether it is done, and re-derives the "[X]"/"[ ]"
checkbox text separately in the list, mark, and unmark branches.

Parallel arrays are easy to let drift out of sync, and duplicating
the checkbox formatting at each call site makes it easy for the
format to become inconsistent. The SE-EDU Java coding standard this
project now follows also expects behaviour to live in well
encapsulated, Javadoc'd classes rather than as loose arrays in the
entry point.

Let's add a Task class holding a task's description and done state,
with markAsDone()/markAsNotDone() and a toString() that renders the
checkbox. YY now stores a Task[] and delegates to it instead of
tracking status separately. Keep Task a plain class for now, since
nothing yet calls for multiple task types.

Add the class- and method-level Javadoc the coding standard requires
to both YY and Task while we're touching them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add support for todo, deadline and event tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The task list stores every user input as an untyped description, so a
task that has a due date or a time span cannot record that information,
and the user cannot tell the kinds of tasks apart when listing them.

Let's add three explicit commands -- "todo <description>",
"deadline <description> /by <when>" and
"event <description> /from <start> /to <end>" -- and show a type icon
([T]/[D]/[E]) alongside the existing done icon.

For this step all three types share the single Task class, which keeps
the change small; the fields that a type does not need are simply left
unused. A follow-up commit will split them into separate classes using
inheritance. Dates and times are kept as plain strings, as the current
requirement does not ask for real date handling.

Adding a task now requires one of the three commands, so unrecognised
input is reported instead of being silently stored as a task.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Use inheritance to model the three task types
commitResults.messageBody:
One Task class carries the fields of all three task types, so every task
object holds unused fields, and toString has to inspect a type icon to
decide which details to print. Adding a fourth type later would mean
adding yet more fields and another branch.

Let's give each type its own class -- Todo, Deadline and Event -- that
inherits the description and done status from Task. Each subclass stores
only the date/time fields it actually needs, reports its own type icon,
and extends toString with its own details, so the type-checking branches
disappear.

Task becomes abstract because a task with no type is not a valid entry
in the list. The list stays a Task[] and calls toString through the
parent type, so polymorphism picks the right subclass behaviour without
the list code knowing which types exist.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add test-ui skill for text-UI regression testing
commitResults.messageBody:
Every check of the chatbot's console behaviour is done by hand, which is
slow and easy to get wrong: the replies differ only by a one-letter icon
or a leading space, so a regression can pass a quick visual check.

Let's record the expected console sessions in test/ui-test-plan.md, with
an aim, an input and an expected output per test case, and add a test-ui
skill that runs them. The runner compiles the sources into a temporary
folder, types each test case's commands on standard input, and compares
the whole session output character for character. It prints the console
input and output of every test case so a run can also be checked by eye,
and it stops at the first failure and prints the expected output, the
actual output and their difference.

The test plan is Markdown so that a test case can be read and reviewed
without reading the runner; the runner parses it, so adding a test case
means editing the plan only. Two placeholders, {{GREETING}} and
{{FAREWELL}}, stand for the fixed start-up and shut-down output, keeping
each expected output focused on the behaviour under test.

The ten test cases cover start-up and exit, adding each of the three task
types, free-text dates, listing an empty and a mixed list, marking and
unmarking, and rejecting an unknown command.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Mandate running the text-UI tests after code changes
commitResults.messageBody:
The test-ui skill and its test plan exist, but nothing says when to use
them, so an agent working in this repository can change the code and
leave the tests unrun and the test plan stale.

Let's state the rule in AGENTS.md, which both Claude and Codex read: after
every change under src/, update test/ui-test-plan.md if user-visible
behaviour changed, then invoke the test-ui skill and show its session
record.

The plan is updated before the tests are run on purpose. Editing an
expected output after seeing a failure turns the test into a record of
what the program does rather than a check of what it should do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList to encapsulate task storage
commitResults.messageBody:
The main method holds the task array and its counter directly, so the
storage representation leaks into every command: adding a task means
assigning to tasks[taskCount] and then incrementing the counter, reading
one means remembering to subtract 1 from the number the user typed, and
the 100-task limit sits in the class that reads commands rather than in
the class that stores them.

Let's move the array and the counter into a TaskList class that offers
add, get and size. TaskList takes the task number the user sees, counting
from 1, and does the index arithmetic once inside get, so the "- 1"
disappears from the command handling and can no longer be forgotten in
one branch but not another.

This is a pure refactoring: the console output is unchanged, and all ten
text-UI test cases still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Split main into one method per command
commitResults.messageBody:
The main method does everything: it prints the banner, loops over input,
decides which command was typed, pulls arguments out of the input string,
updates the task list and prints every reply. That is several levels of
abstraction in one place, so the shape of the program -- read a line,
run a command, repeat -- is buried in string arithmetic, and the reader
has to scan the whole method to find where one command is handled.

Let's leave main with the top-level flow only and give each command its
own named method: printTasks, markTask, unmarkTask, addTodo, addDeadline,
addEvent. Command dispatch moves into executeCommand, which returns
whether YY should keep running, so "bye" no longer needs to break out of
a loop written as "while (true)".

The three add commands each ended with the same three lines of storing
the task and printing the confirmation. That sequence now lives once in
addTask, so the wording of the confirmation and the task count are
produced in a single place.

This is a pure refactoring: the console output is unchanged, and all ten
text-UI test cases still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the command words and argument keywords
commitResults.messageBody:
Every command word is written as a literal twice: once to recognise the
command, as in input.startsWith("todo "), and once to skip past it, as in
input.substring("todo ".length()). The two copies have to agree, so
renaming a command in one place and not the other would leave the program
compiling but stripping the wrong number of characters. The "/by",
"/from" and "/to" keywords are repeated the same way.

Let's declare each command word and keyword as a named constant, and add
hasCommand and getArguments so that recognising a command and removing
its command word are expressed in terms of that one constant. Each
handler now takes only the arguments it needs rather than the whole line,
which also removes the substring arithmetic from the handlers.

This is a pure refactoring: the console output is unchanged, and all ten
text-UI test cases still pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
